Overpayment Scam UK: Do Not Send a Separate Refund

Do not “refund” a claimed overpayment by making a new payment to an account chosen by the buyer. Ask your bank or payment provider to handle it.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-04-30 · Updated 2026-07-10 · 2 min read

overpayment scam UKaccidental overpayment fraudrefund scampayment reversal scamhow to spot overpayment scamsbank transfer scam UKpayment scam UK
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Report it — call Action Fraud on 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland: 101), and forward scam texts to 7726.
On this page
  1. What the scam looks like
  2. Do not rely on a screenshot or message
  3. The old cheque timeline was wrong

What the scam looks like

A supposed buyer, tenant, customer or employer claims to have sent too much and asks for the difference back. The original payment may be a forged screenshot, a fake email, a cheque that is returned unpaid, or money sent from a compromised account. The victim sends a genuine payment and later loses the incoming funds as well.

PayPal’s current scam guidance describes an overpayment scam in which a customer pays more than the purchase price and asks for the difference or postage costs back.

Do not rely on a screenshot or message

Check the account directly through the bank or provider’s official app or site. A payment email, screenshot or balance shown inside a buyer-controlled page is not evidence that money arrived.

Even where funds appear, do not send a new transfer to a different account or method. Contact the provider and ask it to reverse or return the original payment through the original route. Do not release goods until the provider confirms the payment status and advises it is safe.

The old cheque timeline was wrong

The source draft relied on the historical “2-4-6” cheque-clearing rule. UK sterling cheques now use the Image Clearing System. Pay.UK says a cheque paid in before the institution’s cut-off is normally available by 23:59 on the next working day. Bank terms can still include post-payment fraud measures, and foreign cheques or other deposit routes can follow different rules.

Therefore, do not use “day 4” and “day 6” as current general UK advice. Ask the bank about the specific cheque and explain that an overpayment refund has been requested.

Warning signs

  • The supposed payer wants a refund before the provider confirms the payment.
  • The refund must go to a different account, card or person.
  • The buyer sends only screenshots or emails as proof.
  • The payment is much larger than agreed without a credible explanation.
  • Urgent pressure to send the difference, postage or an agent’s fee.

If you already paid

Contact the bank or payment provider immediately, explain both the incoming payment and the outgoing refund, and ask whether funds can be frozen or recalled. Preserve payment references, messages and account details.

Report fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland; in Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101.

Frequently asked questions

Is the 2-4-6 cheque rule still the current standard?

No. UK sterling cheque imaging normally uses a next-working-day cycle, subject to cut-offs, bank terms and fraud controls.

What is the safest way to return a genuine overpayment?

Ask the bank or payment provider to reverse the original transaction through the original route. Do not make a separate payment to details supplied by the buyer.

Does money showing in an account prove it can never be recovered?

No universal statement is safe. Payment type, fraud, bank terms and legal rights all matter. Ask the provider about the specific transaction.
